## The idea

A first Sonic Pi program needs to do more than prove that the speakers work. It should also introduce a distinction that will make later programs easier to understand: the notes and timings describe a phrase, while the synth gives that phrase a sounding body. Those two layers can change independently.

The six-note phrase below rises from E, turns at B, and comes home. Its pitches live in one array and its durations in another. The `play_phrase` function joins the arrays and sends each event to the synth. Start with `:pluck`, because its quick attack makes every onset easy to locate. You can hear where the notes begin before deciding what you think of their colour.

This division between score and renderer is modest here, but it will support much larger examples. For now, listen for two things separately. First follow the shape of the phrase. Then attend to the edge and tail of each note. The contour belongs to the score data; the edge and tail mostly belong to the chosen synth and envelope.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 96
use_synth :pluck

notes = [:e3, :g3, :a3, :b3, :a3, :e3]
durations = [0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1]

define :play_phrase do |pitches, lengths|
  pitches.zip(lengths).each do |pitch, duration|
    play pitch, release: duration * 0.8
    sleep duration
  end
end

play_phrase notes, durations
```

The program schedules six evenly spaced attacks. The first four notes climb, the fifth turns downward, and the final E lasts twice as long as the others. On playback, check whether that extra time gives the last note more closing weight and whether `:pluck` leaves the spaces between attacks easy to follow.

## Change one thing

1. Replace `:pluck` with `:prophet`. The note symbols and sleeps do not move, but the softened attack makes their exact starting points less prominent and the broader tail fills more of the gap between them.

2. Restore `:pluck`, then try `:blade` and `:fm` one at a time. Compare how clearly you can locate each onset. Use words such as *sharp*, *blurred*, *dry*, or *lingering* only when they identify something you can hear.

3. Return to the original synth and change the final duration from `1` to `0.5`. The line reaches the same E, but it no longer pauses there. This separates closure created by pitch from closure created by time.

## Why it works

The arrays are the score. One says which pitches occur; the other says how far the musical clock advances after each pitch. `play_phrase` is the renderer that turns those paired values into scheduled sound. Finally, `use_synth` selects the sound generator. Because each role has a visible home, a one-word synth edit can recolour the whole phrase without rewriting its contour or timing.

Three Sonic Pi instructions carry most of the lesson. `play` starts a sound event. `sleep` advances the thread's musical clock before the next instruction runs. `use_synth` changes the instrument used by later `play` calls. Notice that `play` does not wait for its note to finish. The wait comes from `sleep`, so a note's audible tail and the distance to the following onset are related but distinct.

You can expose that distinction without changing synths. Keep `:pluck` and change `release` from `duration * 0.8` to `duration * 1.4`. The attacks still occur on the same half-beat grid, but each tail now extends past the next attack. The phrase becomes more connected because the renderer changed, not because the duration array changed.

The log pane belongs in this feedback loop. A misspelled synth name stops the program and points to a line; a correctly spelled but unsuitable synth still runs and asks for a listening judgement. Code feedback can establish whether Sonic Pi understood the instruction. Your ears establish what that instruction did to the phrase.

This score-renderer boundary returns throughout the book because it keeps musical questions local. Lesson 2 replaces the note names with integers and transforms them arithmetically, but the playback loop retains the same job. Later lessons will make timing and articulation more elaborate without requiring the pitch data to know how it is rendered.

## Take it further

Add a second six-note phrase and choose four synths that make its contour easy to hear in different ways. Keep one `use_synth` line and one call to `play_phrase`; changing a single synth symbol should still replace the instrument for the whole phrase. This constraint shows whether score data and rendering have remained separate.

Try one deliberate misspelling and copy the resulting log message beside its corrected line. Then run all four valid synths in Sonic Pi 5. For each one, record a concrete observation about attack or decay and note whether the phrase's register suits that sound. Your completed comparison has two reusable phrases, four valid synth choices, and an error you know how to read.
